intro: Financial managers already lead budgets, people and risk, which is why most of their matches are other senior management roles. The closest of the 25 careers below is Sales Managers, with an 83% skill match and a BLS May 2025 median of $148,270, which is 11% less than the $166,570 financial managers earn.
why_it_works: Running finance means planning, forecasting and making calls that the rest of the business depends on. O*NET rates complex problem solving, coordination, judgment and time management at 3.62 out of 5 for this job. Marketing, compliance and executive roles draw on the same planning skills. Because your pay is already high, only 2 matches pay more. The gaps are negotiation and instructing others.
tips: If you want the top seat, chief executives earn $213,990, which is 28% more, though most need a graduate degree.
Marketing Managers earn almost exactly what you do, $166,790, if you want to work closer to customers.
Teach or mentor junior analysts now; instructing is one of your main skill gaps.

faq.q: What jobs can former financial managers do?
faq.a: The closest matches are Sales Managers (83%), Marketing Managers (80%) and Public Relations Managers (78%), based on O*NET 31.0. Compliance Managers are also 78% matched, with a median of $141,900 for their broader BLS group, and use your knowledge of rules and risk.

faq.q: Which careers for financial managers pay more?
faq.a: Only 2 of the 25 matches pay more than $166,570. Chief Executives earn $213,990 (28% more) and Industrial-Organizational Psychologists $193,950 (16% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. Both usually need a graduate degree or many years of senior experience.

faq.q: Do financial managers need another degree to switch?
faq.a: Usually not. 22 of the 25 matches need no more education than financial managers already have, and 3 usually need a graduate degree. A bachelor's degree is common, held by 71% of workers in the closest match, so experience counts most.

faq.q: What skills should financial managers develop?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are operations analysis, instructing, negotiation and systems analysis. Judgment already rates 3.62 out of 5 for financial managers in O*NET, so the step is usually learning to sell ideas and teach others rather than technical finance.
